documents.abstract: Technology flow (TF) forecasting aims to predict whether a technology will be utilized by another, which is significant for future cross-integration technology innovation. Although existing methods have made substantial progress in intra-domain TF forecasting, inter-domain TF forecasting remains underexplored and faces several fundamental challenges. Specifically, semantic gaps between technologies from different domains hinder effective representation learning; historical inter-domain TFs are highly sparse, limiting the ability to learn reliable structural dependencies; and intra-domain and inter-domain TFs exhibit distinct flow patterns, which are difficult to model within a unified framework. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning ( LGCL ) framework that supports both intra-domain and inter-domain TF forecasting. Specifically, we first leverage LLMs with bias-aware representation adjustment to generate semantically enriched and accurate technology representations to bridge gaps across multiple domains. Then, to mitigate the sparsity of inter-domain TF data, a technology co-occurrence view is incorporated to complement historical TF information. We further develop a non-negative contrastive learning module to integrate the TF and co-occurrence views, enabling effective representation alignment without relying on negative samples. In addition, we design decoupled loss functions to separately supervise intra-domain and inter-domain flows, mitigating the difficulty of jointly modeling their different flow patterns under a unified objective. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights into future technology flow trends. Our code is available at https://github.com/huijieliu2023/LGCL .

Antibiotic resistance is a mounting global public health and development threat, with the misuse and overuse of antibiotics driving the rapid dissemination of multidrug-resistant pathogens. Developing next-generation small-molecule antibiotics requires in-depth investigation of resistance mechanisms and the identification of novel targets to overcome the limitations of current treatments. However, current strategies mainly rely on sequence-based homology search or models trained on manually curated datasets, which often suffer from outdated annotations, limited coverage, and high false-positive rates. These limitations hinder the identification of novel resistance targets. To address these limitations, we developed a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered automated pipeline that systematically mines resistance-related knowledge from full-text publications and supplementary materials, thereby supporting scalable and iterative data integration. Building on this framework, we constructed AResDB , a curated resource that integrates data from over 8570 published papers covering bacterial species, compounds, genes, mutations, phenotypes, and quantitative measurements. On this foundation, we constructed AResKG , a large-scale, multi-species knowledge graph of antibiotic resistance integrating 14 entity types, 27 relation types, and over 52.1 million triples. Experimental results based on AResKG demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of commonly used machine learning methods for predicting gene-antibiotic resistance, compared with existing knowledge graphs. This work establishes a scalable, LLM-powered framework for antibiotic resistance research that advances the understanding of resistance mechanisms and accelerates the discovery of next-generation therapeutics.

Steklov eigenfunctions, $\{ϕ_{σ_j}\}_{j=0}^\infty$, are the eigenfunctions of the Dirichlet to Neumann map on a bounded domain with eigenvalue $σ_j$. This paper considers Steklov eigenfunctions and eigenvalues on a family of curvilinear polygons, $Ω_α$ whose boundaries are smooth away from a single corner of angle $α$. We (i) prove optimal lower bounds on the decay of the harmonic extension, $u_{σ_j}$, of $ϕ_{σ_j}$ away from the boundary of $Ω_α$ and (ii) give optimal lower bounds on the degree to which the high energy Steklov spectrum of $Ω_α\setminus H_1$ may differ from that of $Ω_α\setminus H_0$ when $H_1$ and $H_0$ are isometric. This shows that the corresponding estimates in recent work by the authors together with Malagutti are optimal. The proof in this paper was obtained through an interaction with ChatGPT 6 Astra: While writing the work with Malagutti, the authors became curious about optimal error bounds for the difference between the Steklov spectra on a curvilinear polygon, $P$, and the spectrum of any operator which knows only local information about $\partial P$. The authors suggested to ChatGPT to remove two isometric, smooth domains from a curvilinear polygon. ChatGPT suggested the ideas for a proof based on a regularized trace and the singularity in the kernel of the DtN map near a corner. The authors then suggested a simpler, conformal approach, the method for handling small angles, and the idea to obtain lower bounds on Steklov eigenfunctions. The paper is entirely written by the authors and the argument has been significantly modified, clarified, and simplified from the ChatGPT ideas.

Kinematic modeling and path planning are critical problems in intelligent automation that directly affect the precision, adaptability, and safety of robotic arms. The ever-growing complexity of manipulators, including redundant DOFs, unique kinematic architectures, and environmental dynamics, has highlighted the drawbacks of classic analytical and Jacobian approaches in handling singularities, computational costs, and generalizability. Despite many reviews addressing particular problems such as inverse kinematics or reinforcement learning, an extensive overview of methodological development is yet to be provided. The sources for the literature review were mainly obtained from Google Scholar, while the publishing details for the selected articles were then cross-checked using the individual publishers’ and journal sites. The sources are divided into the following nine categories: analytical and hybrid inverse kinematics, neural networks, optimization, deep reinforcement learning, sampling- and learning-based motion planning, diffusion models, trajectory optimization, obstacle avoidance, and imitation learning. From the review, it is evident that there is a shift from traditional approaches such as analysis and optimization to AI-based methods like neural networks, deep reinforcement learning, and diffusion-based systems, with 105 studies published between 2022 and 2026. Some of the findings include MLP-based inverse kinematics (R2 > 0.99), meta-heuristic optimization resulting in a 4.75 × 10−4 cm position error, a 99.4% path-planning success rate through reinforcement learning, diffusion-based visuomotor control, and challenges facing intelligent robotic manipulation research.

This chapter presents the development of machine learning models for short-term energy demand forecasting in academic buildings, using a dataset from a higher education campus in Portugal. The dataset comprises quarter-hourly power demand data collected between January 2016 and February 2020, along with relevant exogenous variables. The study focuses on the impact of hyperparameter tuning on model performance, applying various algorithms—including Random Forest, Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines, Artificial Neural Network, and Support Vector Machines. Grid Search and Random Search techniques were employed to optimize each model’s hyperparameters. Performance was evaluated using benchmarking metrics and visualization tools such as daily load profiles and scatter plots. The results indicate that the Random Forest and Artificial Neural Network models outperformed the others, particularly during school days and examination periods, which represent the most active times on campus. Beyond its technical contributions, this chapter illustrates how machine learning-based forecasting can support energy-aware decision-making in academic buildings, contributing to more efficient and sustainable campus operations. Moreover, the case study presented here highlights the pedagogical potential of integrating AI tools into sustainability curricula, fostering interdisciplinary learning and providing students and researchers with practical insights into the application of artificial intelligence in real-world energy systems.

Trained machine learning models can hold on to traces of the data they were built from, including personal, outdated, incorrect, or unauthorized records. Deleting an entry from a database does not erase what a model has already absorbed from it. Machine unlearning tackles this gap by lowering or removing the effect of chosen training data, ideally without retraining the whole model every time. This review looks at five studies published between 2021 and 2025: one on coded machine unlearning, one on neuron masking, one on zero-shot unlearning, and two wider surveys of methods and evaluation. Together they trace a path from partition-based training designs and changes to model structure toward techniques that still work after the original training samples are gone, accompanied by increasingly systematic taxonomies and metrics. We compare the studies on the data access they assume, the unlearning strategy they use, their efficiency, how well they preserve utility, and how forgetting is verified. We also discuss the main open problems: the absence of a universal evaluation standard, the tension between forgetting and keeping performance on retained tasks, the risk of leftover information, and the difficulty of carrying these methods over to large language models and live systems. The work is a focused narrative review of the chosen papers; no new experiments or benchmark results are claimed. Our conclusion is that machine unlearning is a promising tool for privacy and model governance, but dependable use in practice requires measurable forgetting, clearly stated assumptions, and independent verification.

documents.abstract: If agricultural machinery is to support intelligent, offline assistance, then the system must access technical documentation dynamically. In this paper, the Semantic Synchronization of operator manuals over ISO 11783-based CAN buses is analyzed, defined as the process that brings the local knowledge base of a tractor-side assistant into agreement with the operator manual of the connected implement. Data transfer performance was benchmarked using Markdown, JSON, and XML; various open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) were also evaluated in cross-lingual query tasks. The automatic evaluation of the answers was validated against four human raters. A complete manual was transferred over a physical ISO 11783 network in 31 to 89 s, depending on format and transport settings, which is comparable to the object pool upload that operators already wait for at the first coupling of an implement. Markdown produced the smallest files, while the question-answering performance was comparable across the three formats for most models. With retrieval-augmented generation, locally run models answered most questions on the English manual correctly, with no advantage of the largest model over 7B and 8B models, but performed worse on the five other language editions. Keyword retrieval failed across languages, whereas semantic retrieval provided the cross-lingual capability. The exchange requires only a new parameter group that uses the existing request and transport mechanisms of ISO 11783, which makes it a candidate for standardization. The study is a proof of concept with inference on PC-grade hardware; deployment on embedded agricultural hardware remains future work.

Generative AI is widely framed as democratizing skilled work by lowering the barrier to producing professional output. Drawing on 21 semi-structured interviews with 27 workers across 21 small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) in Kenya and Nigeria (July to October 2023), we find that availability alone did not make participation workable. In participants' accounts, drafting was rarely the hard part. The consequential work was making AI-assisted drafts defensible enough to circulate to clients. We identify five intertwined practices through which participants made generative AI workable: using it as draft labour, steering outputs through iterative interaction, switching and comparing across tools, performing release work to make outputs accountable before circulation, and repairing context misfit when outputs failed local requirements. We make two central contributions. First, we specify release work as a distinct, boundary-facing form of accountability labour, evidenced through verification gates, traceability reconstruction when sources fail, and non-delegation boundaries that decide what can ship. Second, we show how localization and representational failures, which we call context misfit, operate in everyday work as a recurring breakdown-and-repair class, including failures of local language, institutional knowledge, and the credible representation of African people and places, and we document the repair repertoire they demanded. Reframing democratization as workable participation, we argue that reported gains were conditional on this accountability and repair labour, and we translate the findings into four design directions for workplace generative AI. We treat Kenya and Nigeria as two situated cases, not as a representative sample of SMBs or the Global South.

documents.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.

documents.abstract: The use of Conversational Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is growing as a way to interact with health information, especially for the public. This theory-based conceptual synthesis suggests a multilevel governance approach to reducing the likelihood for generated information to become unsafe action – GenAI health information resilience (GenAI-HIR). Its contribution is immediately usable and practical — deploying organizations and public-health actors and public-health actors can use the consequence-based control tiers, actor-specific safeguards, and domain-level audit anchors, and the proposed competency configuration still needs to be validated and is a research agenda for the future. Five conceptually distinct functions at the individual and workforce levels describe at which point protection may contribute to the decision pathway, but are not necessarily assumed to be empirically separable: recognize, interrogate, verify, contextualize, and escalate. Organizational capacity is limited to controls particular to created health information such as authorized sources, attainable human routing, incident monitoring and corrective action. Platform and regulatory conditions are constraints, safety, access, calibrated trust, and equity, outcomes. The framework was created using an expert guided purposive synthesis of the 62 sources that were retained, not a systematic review process. It distinguishes between an explanatory risk model and a normative control architecture and categorizes outputs with respect to type of output, severity, urgency, reversibility, context dependence, mitigation feasibility, and remaining risk. Falsification criteria are now included in six propositions. The candidate self-report indicators are kept as material for the cognitive interviewing only and must be correlated with behavioral vignettes before use for psychometric purposes. GenAI-HIR is therefore not a validated scale, certification standard or replacement for accessible professional care; it is a model for competency that can be falsified in future research and a governance structure that can be audited for current implementation.

documents.abstract: Human rights have become a pervasive vocabulary in Indian legal and social science research, yet the structure and direction of this expanding literature have rarely been examined systematically. This review maps 457 Scopus-indexed journal articles on human rights with at least one Indian institutional affiliation, published between 2016 and 2026, using performance analysis and science-mapping techniques. Annual output grew more than five-fold, from 14 articles in 2016 to 75 in 2025 and 82 in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of about 20.5 per cent. The literature is highly dispersed: the 457 articles appeared in 318 journals, 36 of which account for one-third of the output, and 93 per cent of the 1,516 authors contributed only one article. Citation impact is modest (median one citation; 36.3 per cent uncited; dataset h-index 22). Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies six principal clusters: constitutional equality and discrimination; public health, pandemic and surveillance; artificial intelligence and intellectual property; climate change, displacement and the rights of nature; data protection and international law; and sustainable development and consumer protection. Thematic evolution shows a shift from trade-related intellectual property and health policy in 2016-2020 to COVID-19 and constitutional dignity in 2021-2023, and to artificial intelligence, data protection and climate change in 2024-2026. In contrast, the institutions through which rights are enforced receive very little attention: police, prisons and custody appear in about 2 per cent of articles, caste and Dalit concerns in 2.2 per cent, and the National Human Rights Commission in only three articles (0.7 per cent), none of which takes a commission as its object of study. The review argues that Indian human rights scholarship has undergone a “technological and regulatory turn” that risks neglecting the accountability of the coercive state, and proposes a research agenda centred on enforcement institutions, caste and gender intersections, and data-driven evaluation.

The introduction of innovative products is a critical driver of competitive advantage in highly turbulent technological environments. The objective of this article is to systematically analyze the recent literature on the marketing strategies that optimize the acceptance and performance of such innovations. Using a systematic-narrative methodology, a final corpus of 20 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025 in high-impact databases such as Scopus and Web of Science was selected. The results reveal that commercial success does not reside exclusively in technical superiority, but in the creative configuration of an integrated marketing mix, where packaging design, dynamic pricing, and the diversification of channels toward e-commerce reduce adoption barriers. A strategic shift is identified, moving from traditional launch models toward agile, iterative, and niche approaches that prioritize user co-creation to mitigate perceived risk. Furthermore, functional communication and educational pre-announcements emerge as essential cognitive mechanisms for reducing consumer resistance to change in the face of radical innovations. It is concluded that dynamic organizational capabilities, enhanced by Marketing 4.0 and artificial intelligence, are crucial for personalizing the value proposition and ensuring product sustainability in global markets.

The development of digital technology has enabled the emergence and expansion of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), which are transforming education through global accessibility, flexibility, and interactivity. This paper analyzes several platforms, their structure, the role of mentors, and the application of learning analytics. By searching citation databases and using generative artificial intelligence tools, relevant studies in the field were identified as the foundation of the analysis. An analysis of the most prominent MOOC platforms was conducted, with a more detailed comparison between the international platforms Coursera, edX, Future Learn, and the Croatian national platforms Srce and CARNET. The research shows that platforms differ in their use of technology, target groups, and approaches to mentorship, but they share a common goal: to provide accessible and personalized education. Personalized education is maintained through the role of mentors, reflected in communication on forums, AI assistants, and peer interaction. Learning analytics also play an equally important role, enabling precise monitoring of progress and adapting content to the specific needs of individuals. Alongside many advantages, the paper also discusses challenges such as privacy protection and data accuracy, which influence the development of MOOCs.

documents.abstract: Spreadsheets are the lingua franca of modern finance, driving valuation, forecast, audit, and many other core workflows of the industry. As LLM agents advance to automate knowledge work, spreadsheet construction is a natural and pertinent testbed. However, most existing spreadsheet benchmarks evaluate agents on fill-in-the-blank style tasks, where an agent performs minor edits in otherwise complete spreadsheets. This protocol fails to capture the most central and time-consuming part of the spreadsheet workflow: the modeling decisions, format design, and sheet layout regular knowledge workers need to toil through to build a workbook from scratch. We introduce MBABench-2.0, a benchmark of 101 original spreadsheet construction tasks, the hardest of which is estimated to take 33 hours for a modeler with 3+ years of experience. Unlike coding or math, where a unit test or a final answer can verify an agent's output, the quality of a financial spreadsheet that concerns readability, maintainability, or auditability, is not so simply verifiable. To holistically evaluate spreadsheet construction, we introduce 129 criteria spanning 12 categories that operationalize quality beyond the accuracy of the spreadsheet. Evaluating over 20 agents across 8 models and 4 harness types, we find that frontier agents rarely construct spreadsheets that are both accurate and meet our quality criteria: the top agent achieves a pass rate of only 16% on the benchmark. The benchmark demonstrates a substantial gap in spreadsheet building capability of current agents.

This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within-concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross-lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same-factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out-of-domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity-bearing semantic narrowing from high-probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization-specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence-level and token-local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token-local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.

Open science initiatives have strengthened scientific integrity and accelerated research progress across many fields, but the state of their practice within transportation research remains under-investigated. Key features of open science, defined here as data and code availability, are difficult to extract due to the inherent complexity of the field. Previous work has either been limited to small-scale studies due to the labor-intensive nature of manual analysis or has relied on large-scale bibliometric approaches that sacrifice contextual richness. This paper introduces an automatic and scalable feature-extraction pipeline that combines full-text extraction and human agreement analysis in order to measure code and data availability in transportation research. We employ Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task and validate their performance against a manually curated dataset and through an inter-rater agreement analysis. We applied this pipeline to examine 10,724 research articles published in the Transportation Research Part series of journals between 2019 and 2024. Our analysis found that only 5% of quantitative papers shared a code repository, 4% of quantitative papers shared a data repository, and about 3% of papers shared both, with trends differing across journals, topics, and geographic regions. We found no significant difference in citation counts or review duration between papers that provided data and code and those that did not, suggesting a misalignment between open science efforts and traditional academic metrics. Consequently, encouraging these practices will likely require structural interventions from journals and funding agencies to supplement the lack of direct author incentives. The pipeline developed in this study can be readily scaled to other journals, representing a critical step toward the automated measurement and monitoring of open science practices in transportation research. An interactive explorer can be found on the project page https://www.rerite.org/MOST .

ABSTRACT Hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) is a green oxidant and potential energy carrier, and the photosynthesis of H 2 O 2 from water and oxygen offers a sustainable alternative to the conventional anthraquinone process. Due to the tunable skeletons, adjustable pore microenvironments, and designable active sites, covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and metal‐organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as crystalline porous photocatalysts for H 2 O 2 production. This review summarizes recent advances in COF/MOF photocatalysts for H 2 O 2 production, focusing on density functional theory (DFT)‐based mechanistic insights, descriptor construction, and data‐driven catalyst discovery enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). We first discuss how DFT calculations elucidate active sites, charge‐transfer pathways, and reaction mechanisms by revealing electronic structures, excited‐state charge distributions, adsorption behavior, and reaction free‐energy profiles. We then highlight how DFT‐derived descriptors can bridge mechanistic understanding with materials screening. Finally, we discuss how AI and ML approaches integrate experimental performance, reaction conditions, structural features, and theoretical descriptors to enable candidate screening and design‐rule extraction. Overall, the integration of DFT calculations with AI/ML methods provides a promising route toward mechanism‐guided and data‐driven discovery of COF/MOF photocatalysts for solar‐driven H 2 O 2 production.

This systematic review aims to identify and critically synthesize empirical evidence on the mediators and moderators of the association between artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and self-regulated learning (SRL) among higher education students. Using a theory-informed structured narrative synthesis, the review will evaluate the proposed pathways, consistency of empirical findings, and methodological quality of the available evidence to identify research gaps and inform future investigations in educational psychology.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to transform clinical practice, but its adoption coincides with a longstanding decline in bedside medicine. Herein, we argue that reintroducing Oslerian principles into medical training may be essential to ensure that technological progress does not come at the expense of the physician-patient relationship. Throughout, we use the term AI to refer to tools built on algorithms, from risk calculators and predictive models to large language models, that produce predictions, classifications or recommendations. These tools have no agency of their own: they operate only on the data supplied to them, and their implementation depends on how clinicians and institutions design and deploy them.William Osler never saw an algorithm. He died in 1919, a century before "artificial intelligence" entered the clinical vocabulary. And yet no figure in the history of medicine is better equipped to tell us what we are about to lose 1 . Osler's central achievement was a discipline of the mind: the conviction that the practice of medicine must rest on direct observation of the patient and on the relationship between patient and physician. We argue that this discipline is now under direct threat, and that AI tools, as currently deployed, tend to hasten its erosion rather than reverse it -unless we act deliberately to stop it. In fact, the physician-patient relationship has already been reshaped by decades of patient access to medical information through the internet and social media. This shift has been amplified by the development of health-related AI tools, which increase patients' knowledge but also expose them to misinformation and misinterpretation. Nowadays, patients often arrive at the clinical encounter having already formed their own interpretations about their disease, which directly impacts the dialogue with the physician from the very first minutes of the encounter -a dynamic Osler never had to confront. Oslerian principles must therefore be adapted to this new reality, in which both physician and patient increasingly approach the clinical encounter already shaped by algorithms.Clarifying what AI can do -and will not do in the foreseeable future AI tools can go extraordinarily far in the medical process -synthesizing literature at a scale no human can match, flagging patterns in imaging and pathology that trained eyes miss, drafting notes, triaging risk, generating differential diagnoses, and suggesting therapeutic options in seconds. None of this is in serious dispute anymore, and clinicians who dismiss it outright are being unrealistic.On the other hand, it is illusory to imagine that AI will, in the foreseeable future, replace clinical observation and the personal relationship between doctor and patient. This needs to be said plainly, not hedged. Diagnosis by patternmatching on data is not the same as sitting at the bedside of anxious patients, watching how they behave, picking up on what they leave unsaid, and actually building the trust that makes adherence possible. Whatever level of performance AI models will achieve in the future, they will remain trained on the past, and no model can substitute for what happens, uniquely, in the present, between two people.There is also a more technical reason why bedside medicine remains indispensable: AI can only reason about the reality that has been captured and digitized. An algorithm implicitly assumes that what is absent from the record does not exist. Because important information reaches the record only if a physician observes it, an algorithm working from an incomplete record can return a seemingly precise but inaccurate output, creating an illusion of certainty. Oslerian observation is therefore not a nostalgic complement to AI but a technical prerequisite for its validity: no AI tool can compensate for a hurried or incomplete examination. Far from making clinical skills obsolete, AI demands sharper skills in listening, observation and physical examination.Losing the lessons learned at the bedside is not a hypothetical risk, nor is it a new one. For decades, medical departments have been organized around organ systems and specialized technologies. This process of specialization and subspecialization -a transformation that long predates the current wave of AI adoption -has produced remarkable diagnostic and therapeutic advances, but it has also fragmented the physician's view of the patient as a whole and made a holistic approach harder to sustain. Another powerful driver of this change has been the growth of administrative and documentation burden: in ambulatory practice, a time-and-motion study found that physicians spend nearly two hours on electronic health records and desk work for every hour of direct clinical face time with patients 2 , and administrative burden has been associated with lower intrinsic motivation among physicians and poorer patient-reported experience of care 3 .Consistent with this, studies among internal medicine trainees have documented a clear decline in direct time with patients for well over a decade 4 , and the trend is still underway today in several disciplines. For example, in hematologic malignancies, where AI-based tools are being rapidly adopted to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions 5 , physicians increasingly spend more time in offices in front of computer screens -reviewing algorithmic outputs, multiomic profiles, and risk calculators -often making therapeutic decisions before they examine the patient, so that the consultation risks becoming a confirmation of a decision already made elsewhere, rather than the encounter from which the decision should emerge. Deployed carelessly, AI tools are likely to deepen this pattern rather than correct it. Many current incentives push in that direction: institutions will reward the efficiency of deciding early, physicians will gravitate toward the workflow that is faster and less cognitively taxing, and the tools themselves are easiest to deploy on data that are already structured and available before the visit. Left to market and workflow pressures alone, AI is unlikely to restore the clinical encounter and may further hollow it out. This is the central danger. However, AI can also work in the opposite direction. In a recent randomized trial, ambient AI scribes, which transcribe the consultation and draft the clinical note, were associated with reduced physician burnout, and doctors reported that the technology allowed them to engage better with their patients 6 . Such tools can return the physician's attention from the screen to the patientprovided that the time they free is deliberately protected for the clinical encounter.This is precisely why Osler's teaching should not be treated as an outdated precept, but as the specific countermeasure this moment requires. We argue that it should be urgently reintroduced as a structural component of clinical education, integrated into, not appended to, the technical curriculum. Three Oslerian principles should anchor that effort: "Listen to the patient; he is telling you the diagnosis." What the physician personally learns at the patient's bedside should always come first -a principle physicians in subspecialty training are especially at risk of losing, as AI output can easily become the main input they consult before reaching a conclusion. AI output should inform that conclusion but not replace it."Medicine is learned by the bedside and not in the classroom." Osler's most consequential reform was moving medical education out of the lecture hall and to the patient's side. A century later, the direction of travel has reversed: trainees now often learn to interpret data before they learn to examine a patient. That sequence needs to be corrected, with protected, unhurried bedside time built into training and explicitly shielded from the pressure to consult the algorithm first. "Imperturbability." In his famous 1889 address, Aequanimitas 7 , Osler used this word to describe the calm and steady judgment a physician needs when facing suffering, urgency and clinical uncertainty. Applied to the output of AI, the same discipline must hold: neither adopting it blindly, a failure known as automation bias 8 , nor dismissing it out of hand, but checking it as rigorously as any other clinical evidence, including against what the physician has personally observed.These principles cannot be reintroduced as a simple return to an earlier era; they must be adapted to a clinical environment now shaped not only by AI but also by electronic health records, an ever-expanding volume of diagnostic data, and patients arriving informed -and sometimes misinformed. The task for training programs is not to teach learners to resist these developments but to integrate them without displacing direct observation and reasoning. Concretely, this could include bedside practice that requires trainees to form their own clinical impression before consulting AI output, case studies comparing bedside findings with AI-generated information, exercises showing how omissions in the history or examination alter an algorithm's output, and communication exercises on discussing AI- derived information with patients. These skills should be embedded into formal assessment and not treated as incidental.Discussions on "AI and the future of medicine" too often lead to wishful thinking that is very unlikely to be implemented. Instead, they should lead to concrete proposals, such as treating the clinical encounter as a parameter to be measured in academic medical centers. Time at the bedside is a necessary but insufficient indicator, since more time does not automatically translate into better care. We therefore propose mixed metrics combining the time physicians actually spend with patients, the diagnostic accuracy of the physician working with AI compared with either alone, and patients' perceptions of empathy and trust assessed with validated instruments such as the Consultation and Relational Empathy (CARE) measure 9 .William Osler would have welcomed the advent of AI in medicine, but he would have insisted that every AI tool be held to a single non-negotiable question: does it bring the physician closer to the patient, or does it interpose itself between them? On present evidence, in disciplines already reorganized around screens and algorithms, many AI deployments are failing that test 10 . The remedy is not to slow the technology down. It is to speed up, urgently, the reintroduction of Osler's principles into the training of every physician who will use it.
