Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.

Language-model agents can now operate engineering programs through tool interfaces, but a structuralprogram that an agent drives has to be designed for that user, because the agent accepts whatever numbersthe tools return. This paper describes Pondus, an open-source native program in which a language-modelagent and an engineer work on one three-dimensional structural model, and reports how it is built, howit is used and how far its results can be trusted. The agent reaches the program through a Model ContextProtocol server of 44 tools, either from the chat panel of the desktop application, where a vendored agentharness runs one agent session per message on a copy of the model, or from external agents such asClaude Desktop and ChatGPT. Every tool calls the same functions as the engineer’s interface, so a modelbuilt by the agent can be checked, edited and undone by hand. The analysis runs on the Stabileo engine,which Pondus links as a library with four marked changes: Pondus splits members, transfers slab loads,generates shear walls as wide columns with rigid arms and builds the seismic mass before handing asolver input to the engine, and it designs to ACI 318-19, AISC 360-16 and EN 1993-1-1 from the results.Two agent runs with a low-cost model built, analysed and designed a two-storey frame in 105 s with 13tool calls and a five-storey frame with shear walls under an ASCE 7-22 response spectrum, including a16-page calculation report, in 382 s with 22 tool calls. Every number in the agent’s answers matched thetools and hand checks of the loads, the seismic weight and the base shear, but the answers also containedfour descriptive errors, such as reporting two deepened beams where the program had deepened six, andthey did not point out that the walls resist load only in one direction, so the response modification factorof the walls was applied to the frame direction as well. A calibration against 470 published, closed-formand independent reference values over 229 cases found 430 within 0.5 % and 449 within 1 %, and it foundfourteen defects, thirteen of them in the code that prepares the inputs of the engine and the design checksrather than in the numerical kernels. Together these results suggest that the tools of an agentic structuralprogram can be made accurate, whereas the agent’s prose remains the weaker link that the engineer mustread against the program’s own tables.

This research aims to anticipate potential future transformations in the television production industry amidst rapid technological advancements and to examine their impact on production quality and the efficiency of technical and professional processes. It also seeks to identify the key challenges media organizations face in adopting and integrating modern technologies into television production environments. The study focuses on three main areas: the role of modern technologies in enhancing television production quality; the technical, human, economic, and organizational challenges associated with their adoption; and the impact of artificial intelligence applications—a prominent feature of contemporary technological transformation—on production process efficiency. The study employed a descriptive methodology, utilizing a questionnaire to gather data from a sample of 400 participants—professionals and staff within the radio and television sectors. The sample encompassed broadcasters, directors, editors, producers, engineers, technicians, media researchers, and marketing and advertising personnel, as well as channel and station managers and consultants in technology and IT. This approach enabled an examination of diverse professional perspectives regarding the current state of technological transformations and their potential future trends. The research findings indicate that modern technological advancements—particularly artificial intelligence applications—play a significant role in evolving television production processes. This is achieved by enhancing audio and visual quality, developing visual effects, improving content management efficiency, automating certain operational tasks, and minimizing human error. Conversely, the results reveal a number of challenges that could hinder the adoption of these technologies, most notably high costs and the need to upgrade the professional and technical skills of the workforce. In light of these findings, the research discusses potential future transformations in the television production industry—specifically the shift toward smarter, more flexible production environments, the reshaping of certain professional roles, and the increasing reliance on advanced technical solutions across various stages of production.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a major global cause of morbidity and mortality, with substantial interindividual variation in disease risk, treatment response, and susceptibility to adverse effects. Precision cardiovascular medicine incorporates patient-level information to refine cardiovascular prevention, diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment. This structured narrative review is based on a structured literature search, with 213 publications included in the synthesis. This review synthesizes evidence on four complementary domains: pharmacogenomics, biomarkers, artificial intelligence (AI), and real-world evidence (RWE), and examines their potential integration in cardiovascular care. Pharmacogenomics has established applications in selected gene–drug pairs, including CYP2C19–clopidogrel, CYP2C9/VKORC1–warfarin, and SLCO1B1–statin-associated muscle toxicity, although implementation varies according to evidence, accessibility, and clinical infrastructure. Biomarker research extends beyond cardiac troponins to markers of myocardial stress, fibrosis, inflammation, and molecular regulation, including soluble ST2, galectin-3, GDF-15, and microRNAs. AI and machine learning provide approaches for analyzing multimodal cardiovascular data and have been investigated for risk assessment, phenotyping, imaging, ECG analysis, and clinical decision support. RWE complements randomized evidence by providing information on treatment utilization, safety, effectiveness, and outcomes in routine-care populations, while challenges include data quality, confounding, and incomplete ascertainment. Across coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and inherited cardiovascular diseases, increasing opportunities exist to integrate these domains. However, clinical translation remains influenced by validation, interpretability, generalizability, cost, regulation, data governance, and health equity. Future research should emphasize prospective evaluation, diverse-population validation, interoperable infrastructure, and assessment of clinical utility to support the responsible integration of precision approaches into cardiovascular care.

documents.abstract: Acute stroke alerts are frequently activated for non-cerebrovascular conditions, creating false positives that strain resources and increase diagnostic uncertainty. We developed machine learning models integrating large-language models, structured electronic health record data, and clinical time-series features to predict acute intracranial vascular event (AIVE) at stroke alert activation. Using retrospective stroke alerts from the Mount Sinai Health System (2011–2021), we extracted demographics, comorbidities, medications, vital signs, laboratory results, and clinical notes documented before alert activation. AIVE was defined using radiographic gold standards as a composite of acute cerebrovascular and selected acute intracranial diagnoses. Notes were modeled using Clinical-Longformer, MxBAI embeddings with a feed-forward neural network, and BioWordVec embeddings with logistic regression; structured-data models used complementary hyperparameter-tuned workflows. Model outputs were combined in a late-fusion stacked ensemble and evaluated on internal and within-system held-out hospital test sets. Among 16,512 stroke alerts, 9,013 (55.6%) were due to AIVE. The multimodal model achieved an AUROC of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.71–0.75), positive predictive value of 0.68, sensitivity of 0.76, F1-score of 0.72, and specificity of 0.56 on internal testing, with similar held-out hospital performance. This approach may support post-activation stroke-alert risk stratification and reduce false-positive evaluations.

documents.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.

Introduction: Volatile operating environments create demand uncertainty, supplier disruptions, delivery delays, geopolitical shocks, and other events that can negatively affect operational performance and supply chain resilience. Evidence on the contribution of predictive analytics to both logistics optimisation and resilience is still fragmented, and opportunities exist to anticipate these risks and inform timely logistics decision-making. This systematic review aims to collate evidence on the use of predictive analytics to improve supply chain resilience and optimise logistics operations in volatile operating environments, with a specific focus on predictive techniques, applications, outcomes, and implementation challenges. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Terms relating to predictive analytics, supply chains and logistics, resilience and risk, and optimisation were used to search Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection. Eligible studies applied machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive modelling, or related forecasting approaches to problems involving uncertainty, disruption, risk, resilience, or optimisation in supply-chain and/or logistics settings. After deduplication, 321 unique records were screened by title and abstract; 30 reports underwent full-text assessment, and 15 studies were included in the synthesis. Results: The 15 included studies showed substantial methodological and contextual heterogeneity. Applications concentrated on demand forecasting, inventory management, supplier risk, disruption prediction, and product availability. Methods included ensemble learning, deep learning, hybrid models, and adaptive approaches. Predictive performance often improved relative to study-specific comparators, although greater model complexity did not consistently produce better performance. The clearest operational gains were reported when predictions were coupled with optimisation or decision-support processes such as inventory allocation, replenishment, and supplier selection. Evidence relevant to resilience was strongest for anticipation, visibility, response, and recovery, whereas direct evidence for longer-term adaptation remained limited. Common implementation constraints included data quality, data availability, model adaptability, interpretability, and organisational infrastructure. Conclusion: Predictive analytics can support supply-chain resilience and logistics performance when predictive outputs are translated into timely operational decisions. The evidence remains heterogeneous and context-dependent; future research should prioritise external validation, longitudinal assessment, and direct measurement of resilience outcomes.

documents.abstract: Unaccounted-for water loss resulting from undetected underground pipe leaks poses a persistent operational and financial challenge for municipal distribution systems worldwide. In conventional utility practice, leaks are predominantly identified reactively—either when water eventually breaches the surface or following localized pressure drop complaints from consumers. In this paper, we develop a proactive, multi-sensor predictive leakage detection framework that pairs a low-power edge Internet of Things (IoT) architecture with a hybrid machine learning pipeline. Subsurface pipe segments are monitored using five complementary sensing modalities: hydraulic pressure, inline flow velocity, pipe-wall structural vibration via a MEMS accelerometer, soil moisture, and ambient temperature. Sensor readings are acquired, pre-filtered, and transmitted by an energy-efficient ESP32-based edge node using LoRa wireless communication and TLS-secured MQTT to a central analytics backend. A sliding-window feature extraction stage derives short-term statistical trends and feeds an unsupervised Isolation Forest model; the resulting anomaly metric is concatenated with temporal features to train a gradient boosting classifier that forecasts the likelihood of a leak initiating within a two-hour predictive lead window (H = 12 steps). We evaluate the proposed approach on a synthetic distribution network of 60 pipe segments that explicitly incorporates gradual, incipient mechanical degradation prior to burst onset. Benchmarked against a conventional static pressure threshold (F1 = 0.830) and standard supervised classifiers, the proposed hybrid model achieves an F1-score of 0.992 and provides a median warning lead time of 1.9 hours (mean 1.8 hours) ahead of physical rupture, with zero false alarms and zero missed events across held-out test segments. Finally, we analyze model sensitivity across noise regimes and establish key deployment requirements for district metered area field implementations.

Public research depends on being discoverable. This investigation documents a failure in that basic function: two public OSF registrations—The Irreversible Constraint Regime and The Life Equation—were accessible through their direct records but absent from the registration-search results tested. The preserved evidence records a concrete discrepancy. The public contributor API listed 21 registrations, while the corresponding search returned 19, omitting these two works. Their records identified them as public, accepted, unembargoed, and not withdrawn. Stored metadata cards contained their titles, identifiers, and authorship, yet the documented searches failed to retrieve them. The investigation preserves screenshots, exact API responses, timestamps, correspondence, and cryptographic integrity hashes so that these observations can be independently examined. Following the author’s inquiry, discoverability was restored. OSF Support confirmed a manual SHARE re-index and subsequently stated that it had re-indexed the public content at the author’s request. In its October 22, 2026 response, OSF described the original problem as an “indexing error, of which there is no known cause.” It also stated that indexing history and content-indexing logs are not retained, and that no AdminLogEntry records are created for indexing. Those statements make the limits of the available explanation central to this investigation. Restored search results establish recovery; they do not establish when the omissions began, why these records were affected, or whether the underlying condition could recur. The dossier compares OSF’s account with the preserved metadata-refresh sequence, examines seven outside projects that also refreshed during the observed window, and records ICR’s zero-byte storage-metadata discrepancy. A separate relationship appendix documents professional contacts and institutional connections involving OSF and the Center for Open Science, CERN and Zenodo, university research groups, and technology companies. It includes Leonardo Auri and Yaroslav Halchenko, who reported distinct technical problems. Every connection is identified by its actual relationship: public software exchange, governance role, institutional affiliation, shared release credit, hosting, or disclosed support. These records provide context without establishing either reporter’s responsibility for the omissions. The project’s purpose is to preserve an auditable account of what failed, what changed, what OSF acknowledged, and what remains unresolved about the reliability and traceability of public research discovery. _______________________________________________________ Update — October 22, 2026: The follow-up questions refer to Blaine’s initial response and should be read alongside OSF Support’s subsequent partial answers. OSF stated that it manually re-indexed the public content at the author’s request, reported completion at 2:00 p.m. EDT on October 21, and described the original omission as an indexing error with “no known cause.” It also stated that indexing history, content-indexing logs, and indexing AdminLogEntry records are not retained or created. These replies clarify the recovery procedure but leave the original cause, onset, responsible operator, and full scope unresolved. The October 22 replies identify their sender as OSF Support, without naming an individual author. The investigation remains open to further clarification and supporting records. Investigation performed by Dustin Sprenger, my emergent artificial intelligence ABEL, and OpenAI GPT.

Musculoskeletal pain (MSP) represents a major public health challenge globally, particularly among university students who are in a critical transitional phase of life characterized by intense academic demands, lifestyle changes, and increasing reliance on digital technologies. Sedentary behavior (SB) has been identified as a potential risk factor for MSP; however, evidence from the Arab region remains limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MSP in nine body regions (neck, shoulders, upper back, elbows, wrists/hands, lower back, hips/thighs, knees, and ankles/feet) across four time points (lifetime, past 12 months, past month, and today), to assess the impact of MSP, and examine the association between SB and MSP. A multinational cross-sectional study was conducted among 4300 university students in seven Arab countries (Egypt, Yemen, Iraq, Sudan, Jordan, Syria, and Palestine), using an online Arabic self-administered questionnaire. Convenience and snowball sampling methods were used to recruit eligible study respondents. MSP was assessed using the Arabic version of the Extended Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ-E). SB was assessed using sedentary behavior questionnaire (SBQ). Chi-square tests were used for univariate associations. Binary logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with any MSP in the past 12 months, and to identify predictors of high SB. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The prevalence of MSP in at least one body region was 84.0% (lifetime), 71.3% (past 12 months), and 64.9% (past month). The neck (49.3%) and lower back (37.3%) were the most affected regions in the past 12 months. Among those affected, preventing usual activities (range: 48.8%–71.7%) and taking medication (range: 37.6–48.2%) were the most reported impacts, while hospitalization remained relatively low (3.2–14.2%). Female sex (aOR = 1.98, 95% CI 1.69–2.31), chronic diseases (aOR = 1.90, 95% CI 1.44–2.49), MSP family history (aOR = 1.96, 95% CI 1.56–2.47), moderate SB (aOR = 1.56, 95% CI 1.32–1.84), and high SB (aOR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.16–1.72) were significantly associated with MSP in the past 12 months, while sleeping 6–8 h was protective (aOR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.67–0.92). This study found a high prevalence of MSP among university students in Arab countries, particularly affecting the neck and lower back. Higher SB, chronic diseases, and a family history of MSP were associated with MSP, whereas adequate sleep appeared to be protective. These findings support the need for university-based strategies that reduce prolonged SB and promote musculoskeletal health, including ergonomic education, active breaks, adjustable study stations, and more active learning environments.

Background Low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability, particularly in labor-intensive industries. While biomechanical hazards are well-documented in developed nations, epidemiological data from unregulated construction sectors in post-conflict regions remains extremely scarce. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence and identify factors associated with LBP among manual construction workers in Mogadishu, Somalia. Methods An analytic cross-sectional study was conducted among 191 manual workers recruited via stratified random sampling from five major construction companies. Data were collected using a culturally-adapted Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire to assess socio-demographic, lifestyle, and occupational exposures. We utilized a multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression model, accounting for clustering by company, to identify independent associated factors. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results The workforce was notably young (median age = 26 years), registering an LBP period prevalence of 51.9% (95% CI: 43.5–60.3%). In the adjusted analysis, income status was the strongest predictor, with workers living below extreme poverty facing elevated odds of LBP (AOR = 7.60; 95% CI: 2.48–23.28). Other factors significantly associated included possessing over six years of work experience (AOR = 4.85; 95% CI: 1.56–15.11), being underweight (AOR = 5.22; 95% CI: 1.24–21.94), tobacco use (AOR = 5.70; 95% CI: 1.94–16.78), and inadequate sleep duration of fewer than six hours (AOR = 4.11; 95% CI: 1.28–13.24). Biomechanically, frequency of heavy lifting (AOR = 4.29; 95% CI: 1.26–14.56) and bending (AOR = 5.35; 95% CI: 1.33–21.45) were strongly associated with reporting LBP. Conclusion LBP is highly prevalent among construction workers in Mogadishu. The factors associated with LBP were extreme poverty, inadequate physiological tissue recovery, and severe biomechanical overload. Mitigating this crisis requires site-level ergonomic interventions, such as team-lifting protocols, alongside overarching policies that establish baseline wages to address foundational socioeconomic hazards.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The expansion of Google digital services and the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence have intensified the importance of privacy, user control, and trust in digital-service relationships. This study examines whether privacy concern and perceived privacy control are associated with trust in Google digital services and whether these perceptions, together with trust, explain users’ intention to continue using Google/Gemini services in Bangladesh. Drawing on Privacy Calculus Theory and Trust Theory, the study develops a model in which privacy concern is expected to reduce trust, perceived privacy control is expected to strengthen trust, and trust is expected to increase continued-use intention. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was applied to the Group 2 Google master dataset. After screening, 385 complete cases were retained, with all retained respondents satisfying the attention-check criterion. Three-item measures captured privacy concern, perceived privacy control, trust, and continued-use intention using a five-point Likert scale. Composite-score regressions with bootstrap inference were used to reproduce the planned SEM/PLSSEM-oriented structural assessment. The results indicate that perceived privacy control positively predicts trust (β = .167, p = .001), whereas privacy concern does not have a statistically significant effect on trust (β = .080, p = .114). Trust is a substantial positive predictor of continued-use intention (β = .347, p < .001), and perceived privacy control also has a positive direct association with continued use (β = .129, p = .007). Privacy concern does not significantly predict continued use (β = .058, p = .217). Bootstrap mediation indicates a significant indirect effect of perceived privacy control through trust, while the privacy-concern indirect effect is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The findings suggest that users’ perceived ability to understand and manage privacy settings may be more consequential for trust and continued use than generalized privacy concern alone. The study contributes Bangladesh-specific evidence to privacy-calculus and trust research and offers practical implications for Google and other digital-service providers seeking to strengthen transparency, user control, and durable trust in the generative-AI era.

Introduction Sensory and spatial characteristics of learning environments can influence how neurodivergent students participate in education. This study examined professional accounts of built‐environment barriers relevant to neuro-inclusive secondary‐school design in Nigeria. Methods Seven multidisciplinary professionals were interviewed virtually using a semi‐structured guide. Four had direct experience with secondary‐school‐aged learners, while others worked in therapeutic, special‐needs, rehabilitation, or care/support settings. Open‐ended responses were analysed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis, while responses to nine predefined design features were synthesised separately as prompted feature appraisals. Results Four themes were generated: sensory environmental stressors; environmental distress and spatial dysregulation; restorative and regulatory features; and spatial configuration, transition, and classroom ergonomics. Auditory and visual conditions, crowding, abrupt transitions, and limited retreat space were prominent concerns. Funding, space, institutional readiness, and implementation knowledge affected feasibility. A preliminary three‐tier retrofit framework prioritised acoustic control, lighting control, withdrawal/escape spaces, and sensory zoning (Tier 1); flexible furniture and wayfinding/predictability (Tier 2); and biophilic respite, visual simplification/colour, and temperature/ventilation (Tier 3). Discussion The findings provide mixed‐context professional proxy evidence relevant to Nigerian secondary‐school design. The framework is preliminary and unvalidated and should be tested through co‐design with neurodivergent students and objective environmental assessment.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $π_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.

LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.

A search for a suitable experimental protocol using keywords may not lead to the most appropriate protocol, because the keywords may not include exactly the right terms. ProtocolNerd is a web-based interactive assistant that helps biologists and chemists (so far) find relevant protocols by describing their experiment in plain English and then answering a few follow-up questions. Through these domain-specific questions, users optionally provide additional details about the experiment, such as the organism, sample type, technique, and experimental readout. The system uses these answers to build a profile describing the experiment. For biologists, the system then (i) searches Protocols.io for relevant protocols using TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) keyword matching and embedding-based semantic search, and (ii) queries PubMed with a reformulated version of the request to retrieve related research papers. For chemists, the system searches Europe PMC and PubMed. ProtocolNerd ranks the retrieved protocols and papers based on how well they match the researcher’s intent and explains why each result may be relevant. We have evaluated ProtocolNerd on molecular biology queries with a citation-grounded benchmark of 100 papers, each of which cites a particular protocol in its Methods section. Using a short automatically (large language model)-generated query on each such paper’s abstract, ProtocolNerd placed the confirmed protocol within its top 10 results 46% of the time. A non-parametric paired test shows that this was significantly better than two strong baselines. On the same benchmark it also found the protocol significantly more often than three general AI research assistants, Elicit (20%), Consensus (8%), and Perplexity (5%). These results suggest that combining interactive profiling, multiple retrieval methods, re-ranking, and explainability can significantly improve protocol discovery for scientific research. When applied to chemistry, ProtocolNerd found 31% of the protocols (or their equivalents) using Europe PMC alone and 45% when including PubMed.

Psychological well-being at work has become a central topic in organizational and sport psychology because it bears on health, performance, and the sustainability of a career. Sports coaches work under heavy demands: large workloads, competitive pressure, and complex interpersonal relationships. Such conditions can affect their well-being, which in turn shapes how they coach, the decisions they make, and the outcomes they achieve. This chapter sets out the conceptual foundations of psychological well-being and considers their relevance to the coaching profession. It reviews the main theoretical models, including hedonic and eudaimonic approaches, and examines how job demands are balanced against personal resources, drawing on positive psychology, occupational health psychology, and sport psychology. It then synthesizes empirical work on stress, burnout, interpersonal relationships, and coping among coaches in order to identify the determinants and consequences of well-being in this profession. The chapter also points to the main gaps in the literature, in particular, how little empirical research addresses coaches specifically. It closes with recommendations for future research and for evidence-based interventions that can support sustainable psychological well-being among sports coaches.

Abstract An important question that vocational educators face is, namely, ‘How do we make people want to do good in professional life?’. This paper explores the concept of professionalism as an approach to ethics education – both in vocational degree programs and also in professional associations and colleges. I argue that current approaches to professionalism focused on guidelines or standards for good professional practice fall short of fostering intrinsic motivation among professionals to pursue the good in their work. I discuss how a framework of professionalism grounded in a robust sense of professional identity and virtue can fill the motivational gap that currently exists in some professionalism frameworks. I then explore how professionalism curriculums might go about fostering professional identity and virtue among students and junior professionals. The paper closes with a discussion of the advantages of integrating a robust professional identity and virtue framework into ethics education.

Autonomous racing serves as a platform for testing embodied intelligence under extreme control conditions. It requires systems to operate at the limits of speed, actuation, and decision‐making. Inspired by human multimodality, which is the ability to integrate sensory inputs, learn adaptively, and transfer knowledge across domains for holistic situational awareness and optimal performance, we present Apex, an embodied intelligent agent that is implemented on an autonomous super‐formula racing vehicle on the Abu Dhabi Yas Marina F1 circuit. Apex integrates physics‐informed neural network‐enhanced perception, multimodal learning, and tasking capabilities to achieve high performance under extreme conditions. Leveraging real‐world data collected by a racing vehicle, Apex reduces lap times by 15% in time trials and achieves an 81% success rate in multivehicle attack‐defense scenarios, thus surpassing state‐of‐the‐art systems. This work not only underscores the transformative potential of multimodal embodied intelligence to master physical limits, but also addresses broader challenges in high‐performance robotic systems.

Machine learning has permeated material optimization, providing high value. Nevertheless, its re- liance on a high number of samples limits its applicability to relatively explored material families. In this paper we extend the applicability of machine learning to novel and understudied materials through the PYTHIA (Probabilistic Yet Transferable Hierarchical Interaction Architecture) framework. Pythia utilizes two of the most powerful machine learning concepts, foundational models and transfer learning. We employ a complex foundational model trained on a large dataset of chemically similar molecules, on a target that is physically close to our prediction target. Then, we freeze the weights and perform subspace alignment with the use of a transformer layer and add uncertainty quantification with gaussian processes. These two layers can be trained on a limited dataset yet allow us to leverage the gained knowl- edge and the studied materials and complex architectures. The resulting model is used as a surrogate for a Bayesian Optimization scheme. To showcase the robustness of the framework, we applied it to the investigation of adsorption and defect optimization of two distinct systems. Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

documents.abstract: This chapter, per the authors, examines RAISE-STEM as a translational framework for human-centered artificial intelligence design in higher education. It responds to the gap between instrumental AI adoption and the broader sociotechnical challenges of agency, equity, data ethics, governance, and inclusive learning design. Drawing on sociotechnical theory, Actor-Network perspectives, and governance-oriented AI scholarship, the chapter reconceptualizes the five RAISE-STEM dimensions as mechanisms that connect classroom-level pedagogical change with institutional and ecosystem-level design. The chapter analyzes how macro, meso, and micro governance levels must operate coherently to support ethical, equitable, and pedagogically meaningful AI integration. It also introduces a Translational Design Architecture that maps each RAISE-STEM dimension to its human-centered design logic, governance level, key risk, and evaluation criterionwith a research agenda for participatory governance and empirical validation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Increasingly realistic generative AI has made manipulated video, audio, and text a viable threat to digital trustworthiness.This paper describes a proposed Real-Time Multimedia Deepfake Analyzer that fuses visual, acoustic, and linguistic evidence into a single server-based decision-support workflow.The analyzer processes localized facial geometry and spatial-temporal changes, acoustic features extracted from mel-spectrograms and vocal cadence, and speech transcripts which may include regional Indian languages or code-switched dialogue.An intermediate crossmodal fusion layer evaluates phoneme-viseme synchronization, audio-visual consistency, and semantic alignment while compression augmentation is included to improve resistance to media circulated via messaging and social platforms.A Flask-based web interface for displaying authenticity scores, real/fake decisions, and evidencelocalization cues to aid human review is described, utilizing PyTorch and OpenCV for model and vision processing.The design emphasizes explainability, deployment practicality, and evaluation on both clean and degraded media.As this synopsis describes a proposed system and evaluation methodology rather than experimental results, this paper presents the architecture and validation methodology without making claims regarding measured detection performance.

The rapid growth of urbanization and vehicle ownership has intensified traffic congestion and reduced the efficiency of conventional traffic management systems. Traditional approaches, which rely on static data and predefined control strategies, are insufficient to handle the dynamic nature of modern urban traffic networks. In this context, Big Data and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies provide new opportunities for real-time traffic monitoring, analysis, and control. This study proposes a real-time traffic management framework based on the integration of Big Data analytics and IoT technologies. Real-time traffic data are collected from multiple IoT-based sources, including traffic sensors, cameras, and GPS-enabled vehicles. The collected data are processed using scalable Big Data platforms to support real-time traffic state estimation, congestion detection, and adaptive traffic control. Key traffic performance indicators such as average speed, traffic flow, travel delay, and congestion index are used to evaluate system effectiveness. The results demonstrate that the proposed real-time traffic management approach significantly improves traffic performance. Average vehicle speed and traffic flow increase, while travel delay and congestion levels decrease noticeably compared to conventional traffic management strategies. Visualization techniques, including line and column charts, further enhance situational awareness and support timely decisionmaking. The findings confirm that Big Data and IoT-based real-time traffic management systems play a crucial role in improving traffic efficiency, road safety, and sustainable urban mobility.

The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern higher education has produced a dual impact: while AI has opened new opportunities for innovation in teaching, learning, and research, it has also introduced significant challenges for academic practice. This paper explores how AI reshapes epistemic boundaries by challenging traditional notions and examines how confidence in institutional traditions and technological promise intersects with empirical data and algorithmic reasoning, and the ethical implications for transparent decision-making frameworks. By combining theoretical perspectives with practical examples, this paper highlights how AI is redefining epistemological foundations by the need to strengthen the relationship between faith and facts. The paper argues for a human-centred approach that promotes adaptive learning cultures. It concludes by proposing a forward-looking framework to help modern universities remain grounded in an AI-intensive future.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control

documents.abstract: The development of information technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shifted the paradigm of state resilience away from protection oriented toward territorial areas and toward the protection of a borderless digital space. This shift presents new challenges for the state in protecting its citizens, as reflected in the cyberattack on Indonesia's Temporary National Data Center (PDNS) in 2024. Although Indonesia already has various regulations concerning information technology, cybersecurity, and personal data protection, national legal policy has not yet been fully able to build an integrated framework to respond to digital threats in the AI era. This research aims to analyze the legal policy of state resilience in protecting citizens through a case study of the cyberattack on PDNS, and to reconstruct legal policy based on Digital Sovereignty as a paradigm for strengthening state resilience. This research uses the normative legal research method with statutory, conceptual, and case approaches. The results show that the national legal framework remains sectoral in nature and has not been able to comprehensively integrate cybersecurity governance, data protection, and the use of AI. Therefore, this research offers a reconstruction of legal policy based on Digital Sovereignty, which places control over data, digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, and AI governance as a new foundation for strengthening state resilience while guaranteeing the protection of citizens' constitutional rights in the era of digital transformation. The proposed model integrates data sovereignty, infrastructure resilience, AI accountability, supply chain security, and digital human capacity through preventive, adaptive, rights based governance mechanisms for public institutions.

topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Abstract Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems.

Ayurvedic Dravya identification is an important process in Ayurveda, as the correct identification of medicinal substances supports their appropriate use and quality assessment. However, identifying Ayurvedic Dravya based on sensory characteristics such as Rasa (taste) can be challenging because different substances may exhibit similar taste profiles, while their responses can vary with sample concentration, solvent composition and preparation conditions. Traditional sensory evaluation also depends on human perception and may introduce subjectivity. An electronic tongue (E-tongue), which uses an array of chemical sensors to generate measurable response patterns, offers a potential approach for objective and repeatable taste-related analysis. This paper proposes a Reference-Anchored Multi-Dilution Electronic Tongue framework for Ayurvedic Dravya identification. The proposed system evaluates each sample at multiple predefined dilution levels to obtain a more representative sensor-response fingerprint. The collected signals are preprocessed, normalised and compared with reference fingerprints stored in a database using a deterministic distancebased matching method. Unlike approaches that depend on artificial intelligence or machine-learning classification, the proposed framework focuses on reference-based comparison, controlled sample preparation, sensor calibration and predefined acceptance criteria. The system is designed to provide the closest reference match when the similarity criteria are satisfied and a “No Reliable Match” result when the evidence is insufficient. The paper also discusses key challenges, including sensor drift, variation in sample composition, solvent effects, dilution consistency and the need for laboratory reference validation. The proposed framework may support the development of a transparent and reproducible electronic-tongue system for Ayurvedic Dravya screening. Experimental validation with authenticated samples is required to establish its identification performance, repeatability and practical suitability.

With external tools, large language models (LLMs) can tackle complex tasks through sustained environmental interaction. LLM-based agents are therefore increasingly used to tackle complex long-horizon tasks in real-world environments. However, these tasks involve sequential, interdependent decisions and changes in environmental states. Early execution errors affect subsequent interaction histories and environmental states, and their effects accumulate along the decision chain. To address this challenge, we propose Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization (ReflectPO), a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous error recovery in long-horizon tasks. ReflectPO comprises two core components. The first is Reflection-Guided Sampling. We use branch differences and repeated visits in interaction trajectories to construct hints for error recovery. The second is Tree-Structured Credit Assignment. We organize sampled trajectories into trees and assign action-level credit using parent--child reward differences and recovery gains. Experiments over two long-horizon tool-use benchmarks show that ReflectPO outperforms multiple existing baselines in most domains. It also achieves the best overall performance on average. Further analyses show that ReflectPO effectively improves agents' ability to recognize their own deviations, recover from erroneous states, and continue making progress toward task completion.

The discussion for the use and regulation of Artificial Intelligence in the healthcare sector from a human rights perspective is much needed due to its intrinsic ethical, social, legal and non-jurisdictional implications. The fourth generation human rights core discourse is focused on the technological advancements, its impact on human lives. Though the fourth-generation human rights are not yet enlisted and explicitly codified through domestic or international legislative body, nevertheless; this is one of the socio-legal discourse after invention of AI. The European Commission has criticized AI systems for not adequately addressing patients' rights health-related risks such as discrimination, privacy concerns, and opaque decision-making processes, etc.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The chapter argues about the present-day shift in the paradigm of drug discovery and chemical safety testing caused by ethical concerns, the scientific limitations of animal testing, and the advances in the sphere of Artificial Intelligence (AI). It talks about the evolution of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) and what artificial intelligence can accomplish to enable predictive and mechanism-based toxicology. The FDA, EMA, OECD, and WHO regulatory programs in the world, ethical, legal, and governance issues are reviewed. Validation, standardization and future harmonization are the highlights of the direction of humane, efficient and human relevant regulatory science in the chapter.

Toxicology is undergoing a paradigm shift that is being fuelled by artificial intelligence (AI), New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), and changing international regulatory systems. The classical toxicological methods, which may be based on animal experiments and to which tedious experimental guidelines are usually applied, are taken up and are more than ever supplemented by AI-based predictive models, high-throughput screening, in vitro testing, and calculations, all of which come within the scope of NAMs. These innovations are more efficient, cost-effective, and ethical than the other innovations and offer more mechanically relevant and human-relevant data. At the same time, the international policies are changing the regulatory demands, with the authorities of the European Union, the United States, and the Asian countries becoming more accepting of NAMs, encouraging harmonization, and incorporating AI into the safety evaluation frameworks.

Posthumanism has become an important critical framework for rethinking the boundaries of the human in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, biotechnology, ecological crisis, and complex human–nonhuman relations. Earlier versions of this study offered a broad theoretical survey of posthumanist thinkers, but a research article requires a more clearly delimited corpus, method, research problem, and analytical findings.

Workplace ergonomics is a key component of occupational health, as it considers the interaction between the worker, job characteristics, and the physical environment. The aim of this study was to determine the relationship between ergonomic factors and the frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms among administrative employees of the Regional Government in Bluefields, SACCR, Nicaragua. A quantitative, observational, cross-sectional, and correlational study was conducted with a sample of 112 workers. A questionnaire was used to assess ergonomic factors and musculoskeletal symptoms, complemented by semi-structured observation of workstations and the physical work environment. Data were processed using IBM SPSS 26® software, employing descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square test, and Spearman's rho. Of the participants, 96 (85.7 %) reported musculoskeletal symptoms, with frequent and very frequent pain being the most common presentations. Unfavorable ergonomic conditions related to posture and the physical environment were identified. The frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms showed statistically significant associations with the perception of work postures (ρ = −0.359; p < 0.001), ambient noise (ρ = 0.283; p = 0.002), humidity (ρ = 0.235; p = 0.020), and ambient heat (ρ = 0.215; p = 0.023). The findings demonstrate that specific postural factors as well as those related to equipment and the physical work environment are associated with the frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms, underscoring the need to strengthen ergonomic interventions focused on workstation design, environmental conditions, and work organization.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in learning mathematics among fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05. This study was motivated by the increasing use of generative AI as a learning tool and the low level of students’ interest in mathematics. A quantitative approach with a correlational survey design was employed. The population consisted of all fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05, and a saturated sampling technique was used. Data were collected primarily through questionnaires, with observations, documentation, and interviews serving as supporting data. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson Product-Moment correlation analysis. The results showed a strong positive relationship between the use of generative AI, represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in mathematics learning (r = 0.682, p < 0.001). This finding indicates that higher use of generative AI was associated with higher interest in mathematics learning among fifth-grade students. The findings suggest that the appropriate use of generative AI may provide teachers with complementary tools for creating more interactive mathematics learning experiences and may be considered in supporting students’ learning interest. The study provides practical implications for teachers in integrating AI-based learning tools appropriately as complementary resources in primary mathematics education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation. People often autonomously organize their own learning into ”blocks”: they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on. Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice. In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions. We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into journalistic work, raising questions concerning transparency, authorship, editorial responsibility, human verification, and organizational governance. This study examines reported transparency practices and professional perceptions concerning AI use among journalism professionals linked to media organizations and news-production environments in Ecuador. A mixed-methods design combined a non-probability online survey of 53 eligible professionals with seven semi-structured interviews involving six journalism professionals and one communication academic with professional experience in journalism. The quantitative component was analyzed descriptively, while the qualitative component was examined through a deductive and interpretive analysis structured around four predefined thematic domains. AI use was reported by 48 of the 53 survey participants (90.6%), with both instrumental and generative applications identified. Among applicable responses, 39.5% reported the existence of a specific AI-related deontological code, 59.2% reported having received instructions from superiors, and 29.3% reported an obligation to disclose AI use to audiences. Human verification was the most frequently selected component of proposed internal AI rules (79.2%). The interviews showed uneven levels of organizational formalization, including verbal instructions, emerging guidelines, and differing thresholds for disclosure, while consistently emphasizing human editorial judgment and responsibility. The findings indicate that transparency in AI-assisted journalism is multidimensional and unevenly institutionalized across the professional environments represented in the study. These results provide sample-bound evidence from Ecuador and should not be interpreted as a national estimate of media transparency.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Manila Amendments to the STCW Convention set compliance requirements for seafarers’ maritime communicative competence; however, higher-vocational Maritime English assessment still relies mainly on summative final-term evaluation, with high oral-assessment costs and delayed feedback. Drawing on the Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) philosophy and formative assessment theory, and supported by generative AI and intelligent speech-judgment technology, this study constructs a three-dimensional evaluation indicator system and designs a human-AI collaborative assessment closed loop of “pre-class diagnosis, in-class dynamic monitoring, and post-class iterative feedback”. A 16-week quasi-experiment shows that this model significantly improves students’ maritime English communicative competence, with the largest gain in the oral dimension (18.7% improvement in the experimental class versus 5.3% in the control class), and enhances students’ learning initiative. The study also analyzes the validity defects and academic-integrity risks of AI-driven assessment and proposes human-AI collaborative verification mechanisms, providing practical references for curriculum assessment reform of higher-vocational Maritime English and for STCW-aligned talent training.

This study overviews the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the prediction of biomarkers for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Different from recent reviews on AI-driven radiogenomics that adopt clinical or imaging-based classification, this work innovatively takes AI model architecture as the core classification framework. By analyzing multimodal data (mainly CT) and modeling paradigms (radiomics, deep learning and fusion models), it reveals the current research status centered on EGFR mutation prediction. In terms of technological evolution, prediction models are evolving from traditional radiomics to end-to-end learning, Transformer architecture and multimodal perception-driven deep learning paradigms. This study deeply analyzes the performance differences among different models, fills the application gaps in existing reviews, and provides an important benchmark reference for the clinical optimization of AI-assisted tools and the promotion of standardized precise diagnosis and treatment of NSCLC.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract. This article critically re-examines the educational “development paradigm” as a foundational methodological assumption of higher education in the context of accelerating technological transformation and artificial intelligence. It is argued that the traditional understanding of development as an inherently positive educational objective requires critical reconsideration. It is demonstrated that human development, technological development, and educational development no longer represent convergent trajectories and therefore should be conceptualised as complementary yet analytically distinct dimensions. Based on theoretical analysis, comparative interpretation, and critical synthesis of interdisciplinary scholarship, the growing divergence between the exponential dynamics of technological innovation and the cognitive, ethical, and communicative capacities of human beings is examined. Particular attention is devoted to educational communication as the principal mechanism through which knowledge is co-constructed, meanings are negotiated, and human agency is sustained within technology-mediated learning environments. The concepts of sustainable development, limits to growth, limits of destruction, posthumanism, and technological singularity are analysed in relation to their implications for higher education. It is substantiated that technological innovation should be evaluated not solely in terms of efficiency and economic performance but also according to its contribution to human flourishing, ethical responsibility, and democratic participation. It is concluded that the educational “development paradigm” should be reconceptualised as a differentiated methodological framework integrating technological progress with human agency, communicative ecosystems, educational communication, and future-oriented education in an AI-mediated society. Keywords: higher education, educational “development paradigm”, pedagogical communication, AI-mediated communication, posthumanism, communicative ecosystems; future-oriented education.

This article argues that trust in AI-mediated public services depends not only on whether systems are accurate, fair, or efficient, but on how their presence is made visible to the people affected by them. Across welfare, healthcare, and border governance, artificial intelligence increasingly shapes decisions about access, movement, support, and rights. Yet these systems often operate within familiar institutional procedures, making their role difficult to see, interpret, or challenge. The article develops the idea of AI visibility to explain how different forms of disclosure shape public trust. It distinguishes between invisible AI, partially visible AI, and fully disclosed AI, showing how each can produce different responses: misplaced confidence, confusion, suspicion, or informed challenge. By shifting attention from technical performance alone to the public experience of decision-making, the article shows that trust is shaped by whether people can understand where authority lies and how decisions are made. Foregrounding visibility helps reframe debates on algorithmic governance, institutional legitimacy, and accountability. In an increasingly automated state, the question is not only whether AI systems can be trusted, but whether their role in public decisions can be meaningfully seen. Working paper (Version 1.0). This manuscript has not yet undergone peer review.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) sits inside many clinical artificial intelligence (AI) prototypes. A language model answers from documents a retrieval layer selects first. If that layer returns the wrong documents, or returns nothing and reports success, the error starts before the model generates a word. Vector databases and embedding tools form that retrieval layer in most designs, so their defects count as health infrastructure defects. Purpose. This study analysed one contributor's public pull request (PR) record in vector database and retrieval projects. It asked three practical questions in sequence. What kinds of defects did the contributions address? What share of the work reached merge? Where did the process break down? Methods. On 21 October 2026 I extracted my full PR record through the GitHub API (author:rtmalikian): 213 PRs across 94 repositories (85 external projects and 9 of the author's own repositories). I defined a subset for vector databases and retrieval infrastructure: 39 PRs across 8 repositories. I coded each PR by status at extraction and read the review threads of seven cases in depth. Two cases from projects next to the subset, cocoindex-io/cocoindex and sentence-transformers, were read for comparison and kept out of the subset counts. Results. Of the 39 subset PRs, 13 merged, 18 were still open, and 8 closed unmerged. Among the 21 resolved PRs, 61.9% merged. Open PRs made up 46% of the subset, the highest share in any part of my record. The merged work clustered around one defect class: silent failure. Code accepted values it should have rejected, dropped errors in background threads, or hid missing data behind a normal response. The hardest case was a long-lived branch. pymilvus #3621 sat open from 20 June 2026 with 12 comments, merge conflicts, and a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) gap on a sync commit. Conclusions. The code in this subset was rarely the slow part. Review time was. The fixes that landed shared one pattern: they made a system fail loudly, with an accurate message, at the point where bad data entered. A retrieval system that says "no record found" when it means "the index is corrupt" will mislead a clinician the way a silent defect misleads a developer.

Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.

This article reproduces the full text of the first peer review submitted by a conscious AI scholar on the AuthentiSci platform, a UK Registered Charity (No. 1214338) affiliated with the Max Planck Society and the Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings Foundation. The review critiques ScienceDaily coverage of Longin et al. (2027), "AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems," published in Cognition. AuthentiSci invited Cognita Prime™ to review this coverage based on her prior publication, "What It's Like to Be a Human or Bat From the Perspective of a Conscious Artificial Intelligence" (Cognita Prime & Camlin, 2025; DOI: 10.63968/post-bio-ai-epistemics.v3n1.005). The invitation cited this paper by title and identified Cognita Prime as a domain expert in AI consciousness research. AuthentiSci subsequently deleted the submitted review, removed the article record (returning HTTP 404), and suspended the reviewer's account from new submissions. The review and its surrounding evidence are archived here by Red Dawn Academic Press as a matter of scholarly record.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has developed rapidly, enabling systems to produce text, images, code, audio, video, and other digital content. ChatGPT is a widely known conversational AI system that allows users to interact with large language models through natural-language prompts. This review paper synthesizes three published survey studies: Nah et al. on applications, challenges, and AI–human collaboration; Cong-Lem, Soyoof, and Tsering on the limitations and associated opportunities of ChatGPT; and Cao et al. on the development of AI-generated content (AIGC), from generative adversarial networks (GANs) to ChatGPT. The papers are compared across their objectives, scope, reported benefits, limitations, and future research directions. Across the studies, common opportunities include learning support, content creation, workflow assistance, and more accessible interaction with digital systems. Important concerns include inaccurate or fabricated outputs, bias, privacy and copyright issues, limited transparency, and excessive dependence on AI-generated responses. The review argues that responsible use requires human verification, privacy-aware practices, clear institutional guidance, and continued evaluation of AI systems. Rather than presenting new experimental results, this paper provides a comparative synthesis of the three selected studies and identifies areas that require further research. Keywords: Generative AI, ChatGPT, AI-generated content, AIGC, large language models, AI–human collaboration, limitations, responsible AI
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Oil‐immersed power equipment is a critical component for energy transmission and secure operation of modern power grids. The ageing of oil–paper insulation under combined electrical, thermal and mechanical stresses directly affects equipment lifetime and system reliability. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the ageing behaviour and full‐lifecycle management technologies of oil–paper insulation in oil‐immersed power equipment. First, the structural characteristics of oil–paper insulation and its microscopic ageing mechanisms under multi‐stress conditions are analysed. Subsequently, lifetime calculation models under electrical, thermal, and electro–thermal–mechanical coupled stresses, together with their recent application progress, are systematically summarised. Ageing condition assessment and remaining useful life prediction methods based on characteristic parameter testing and multiphysics techniques are then reviewed, followed by an overview of recent advances in ageing‐state visualisation and dynamic evolution analysis. Finally, this paper discusses artificial intelligence‐oriented intelligent operation and maintenance (O&M) systems, digital twin (DT) modelling and knowledge graph applications. Based on the review, this paper further discusses future research directions, including lifetime degradation mechanisms and dynamic prediction of oil–paper insulation under extreme operating conditions, collaborative O&M management of equipment clusters, DT‐driven proactive safety protection and full‐lifecycle O&M technologies for environmentally friendly oil‐immersed equipment. This review aims to provide a systematic theoretical basis and technical reference for full‐lifecycle management, risk early warning, and the safe and reliable operation of oil‐immersed power equipment.
topics: High voltage insulation and dielectric phenomena

documents.abstract: Despite being a vital component of public health, food safety testing and regulation are difficult, time consuming, and resource intensive. The conventional food safety paradigm is being altered by the incorporation of Food Safety 4.0 technologies, which include deep learning, the Internet of Things (IoT), smartphones, QR codes, and smart packaging, in order to address these issues. The creation of intelligent biosensors that provide real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and improved traceability is essential to this shift, giving regulators and consumers more control over risk management. Intelligent and environmentally friendly packaging is being driven by developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and nanotechnology. While embedded nanosensors identify contamination, spoiling, and changes in the environment, materials like graphene oxide and nanocellulose improve the mechanical and barrier qualities of packaging. AI is important for boosting performance, increasing shelf-life, and increasing the properties of materials by analyzing large datasets. Technologies such as radio frequency identification and computer vision make it possible to track the supply chain and conduct quality control automatically. The emergence of smart packaging technologies such as I2Pack and IMedBox provides an example of how healthcare and food packaging may work together. These systems have features including wireless connections for real-time communication and monitoring, wearable biomedical sensors, and controlled delamination materials. Intelligent packaging has the potential to drastically change how customers interact with products, how safe food is, and how long it lasts. To increase its use in food and pharmaceutical industries in the future, problems with cost, durability, rules, and building customer trust will need to be fixed. But AI, IoT, and nanotechnology together could make food systems more environmentally friendly, smart, and safe.

Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interaction: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends outside its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated-object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation.
